title: Canal colonies
hook: new canals turned dry land green and Sikh farmers moved west to farm it

segments.voice: Yesterday, granthi, and your line was far-off service. Today, the men who stayed with the land, and a land that changed under them.

Dry ground, cracked and pale, with thorny scrub and not much else. Herders cross it with their animals. Rain is rare. Then a channel of water arrives, cut straight across the plain, and the ground on either side darkens. Within a few seasons there is wheat where there was dust, and a family from a crowded village in central Punjab is standing in a field that, a few years before, was nobody's farm at all.
screen: `DRY GROUND AND THORNY SCRUB.` → `A CHANNEL OF WATER ARRIVES.` → `WHEAT WHERE THERE WAS DUST.`

segments.voice: In western Punjab, between the rivers, lay wide dry uplands that people called the bar. British engineers dug canals from the rivers across this land, and where the water went, farms could grow. The government granted the new land to families brought in from other parts of Punjab. Sikh farmers were among them, leaving crowded home villages for bigger plots out west. They built houses, wells and gurdwaras, and whole new villages grew up around the canals. New market towns were laid out to serve the colonies. One of them, Lyallpur, was planned with bazaars running out from a clock tower at its center. Today that city lies in Pakistan, and how Sikh families left these lands is a later, harder story. For now, it was a story of water and wheat. The salok at the close of the Japji names the world as a family: air is the Guru, water is the father, and the great earth is the mother. In the colonies, farmers could watch that line take shape, water making fields out of dust. No crop grew on that plain until the water came, and a farmer's whole year hung on the canal running on time.
screen: `CANALS ACROSS THE DRY BAR.` · `SETTLERS FROM CENTRAL PUNJAB.` · `A TOWN AROUND A CLOCK TOWER.` · `WATER IS THE FATHER.` · then, large: `WATER MADE FIELDS.`

segments.voice: Look at some water if you can, a glass on the table, a tap, rain on a window, a river from a bridge, or picture the last water you saw. Follow it back in your mind, a reservoir, a pipe, a cloud, a river, and the fields it might have passed on the way, and let yourself feel the size of it for a moment. If you pray, say Waheguru as you look.
Canal colonies. Dry land in western Punjab, watered by new canals and settled by farming families, Sikhs among them, who built villages, wells and gurdwaras there. Today's word.
Your line: water made fields. Water is the father, the Japji says, and the earth the mother. Day nine hundred fifty.

howItsDone: Sikh families from the old canal colonies of western Punjab still tell stories of the villages their grandparents built there, and Sikhs who recite the Japji in the morning end it with the salok that names water as the father.

chat.says: Why did Sikh farmers move west in British Punjab?
options: New canals turned dry land into farms, and settlers were granted bigger plots there.
The rivers in central Punjab dried up, so every farmer had to leave the village.
The army ordered them west to guard the frontier and paid them in land.
chat.meaning: Canals carried river water across the dry bar; the land was granted to settlers, Sikh farmers among them, who left crowded villages for bigger plots.

notes: No dates or settler numbers given. The outline hook says 'many Sikh farmers moved west'; the voice says 'Sikh farmers were among them'. Confirm.
Lyallpur (now Faisalabad) described as planned with bazaars running out from a clock tower; confirm.
The phrase 'how Sikh families left these lands is a later, harder story' points ahead to Partition without detail; confirm a Keeper is comfortable with the forward reference.
Japji closing salok (pavan guru paani pita maata dharat mahat) paraphrased; confirm Ang 8.
Source attribution (Imran Ali) is for a Keeper to check or replace with a preferred history.
Editor: the Japji's closing salok is no longer attributed to Guru Nanak by name in the voice, since a version of it also appears under Guru Angad's name (Ang 146); confirm the preferred attribution.
